Walk through any Nigerian market at harvest time and you will see the problem. Tomatoes, pepper, plantain and cassava arrive in huge quantities, prices crash, and a lot of food goes bad before it is sold. A few months later the same produce is scarce and expensive. **Small-scale food processing** is the skill of turning that cheap, perishable harvest into a product that keeps for weeks or months, so you can sell it when buyers are ready and at a better price.

Fresh food spoils for three main reasons. **Microorganisms** (bacteria, moulds and yeasts) feed on the moisture and nutrients in food. **Enzymes** inside the food itself keep working after harvest, softening and browning it. And **pests and physical damage** (insects, rodents, bruising) open the door to both. Every processing method you will learn in this course works by slowing or stopping one or more of these.

What 'adding value' really means

Adding value means the money you earn from the finished product is higher than the cost of the raw food plus everything else you spent on it: fuel, oil, packaging, labels, transport and your own time. A product can look profitable until you count the nylon, the gas and the hours. You will learn full costing in Module 3. For now, think in simple terms: raw cost in, finished value out, and the gap must be worth your effort.

The science of keeping food: water, heat, acid, salt and sugar
Explain how drying, heating, acidity, salt and sugar stop spoilage
Describe water activity and why 'dry to the touch' is not enough

Microorganisms need four things to grow: **water**, **food**, **warmth** and **time**. Most also need the food to be not too acidic. Every preservation method takes away at least one of these. When you understand which one your product relies on, you know exactly which step you must never rush.
Water: the most important factor

It is not just how much water is in a food, but how much is **free** for microbes to use. Scientists call this **water activity** (written aw), measured from 0 to 1. Pure water is 1.0. Fresh fruit is close to 1.0. Most harmful bacteria need a water activity above about 0.85 to 0.90, while some moulds can still grow at lower levels. Properly dried foods such as dry garri, crisp chips and well-dried pepper sit far below these levels, which is why they keep.

You will not usually own a water activity meter, so you use practical tests: dried pepper should snap, not bend; dried okra should be brittle; garri should flow freely and not clump; chips should crunch, not chew. If a product bends or feels leathery, there is still enough water for mould.
A bright sun
Sun and heat drive off water, the main thing microbes need to grow.
Heat, acid, salt and sugar

**Heat** kills most microorganisms and stops enzymes. Roasting garri and groundnuts and frying chips all use heat. But heat alone does not protect food once it cools and is exposed again, so packaging must follow.
**Acid** slows bacteria. Foods with a pH of 4.6 or below are classed as high-acid. Fermented garri becomes slightly sour, which helps it keep.
**Salt** pulls water out of food and out of microbes. It is used in dried fish, salted vegetables and some spice blends.
**Sugar** works like salt by binding water. Jams and syrups depend on a high sugar level.
Do not bottle low-acid foods in oil or water at home

Low-acid foods such as pepper, garlic, onion or vegetables sealed in oil or water, without proper acidification and tested heat processing, can allow Clostridium botulinum to grow and produce botulinum toxin, which can kill. You cannot see, smell or taste it. Stick to dry products in this course unless you receive proper training and lab support.
Following the science through garri

Garri is a good teaching product because each step has a clear job. Fresh cassava roots contain natural compounds (cyanogenic glucosides) that can release cyanide. Traditional processing reduces them to safe levels, but only if steps are not skipped.
How cassava becomes garri
Peel and wash roots
Grate into mash
Bag, ferment and press
Sieve the cake
Roast while stirring
Cool, sieve and pack
Grating, fermenting, pressing and roasting together reduce cyanide and moisture.
**Peel and wash** within a day or two of harvest. Cassava roots spoil fast, so delay means rot.
**Grate** into a fine mash. Grating breaks the cells so natural enzymes can begin breaking down the cyanide compounds.
**Bag, ferment and press** for usually one to three days. The liquid drains out and takes some cyanide with it, and fermentation gives garri its sour taste.
**Sieve** the pressed cake to remove fibre and lumps.
**Roast** (garify) in a wide pan over steady heat, stirring constantly until it is dry and crisp. This drives off moisture and remaining cyanide. Some producers add palm oil for yellow garri.
**Cool, sieve and pack** in clean, dry bags. Packing while warm causes condensation and mould.
Worked example: reading a failed garri batch
For example, Bisi in Ogun State pressed her mash for only half a day because a buyer was waiting, then roasted it quickly on high heat.
After a week her garri had small lumps and a stale smell.
She checked her notes: short pressing time meant extra water stayed in the mash.
High heat browned the outside of the granules before the inside was dry.
For the next batch she pressed for two full days and roasted on medium heat, stirring longer.
The new batch flowed freely, stayed crisp in a sealed bag and had the familiar sour taste. Rushing pressing and roasting had left both water and risk behind.
Matching the method to the food

Plantain chips rely on frying to drive out water and on airtight packaging to keep humidity out. Groundnut paste relies on roasting and on very low water, but its fat can go rancid, so it needs clean, tightly closed containers away from heat and light. Pepper blends rely entirely on thorough drying before grinding. Dried okra and tomato rely on drying and on protection from insects. In each case, the moment moisture gets back in, the protection is lost. That is why the next modules spend so much time on cooling, packaging and storage.
Use the same logic for any product: name the factor your method controls (water, heat, acid, salt or sugar), then protect that step from shortcuts.

Hot oil and gas

Never leave frying oil unattended. If oil catches fire, turn off the gas if you can do so safely, cover the pot with a lid or fire blanket and leave it covered until cool. Never pour water on burning oil: it explodes into a fireball. Keep children away from the frying area and keep gas cylinders upright, outside or in a ventilated place, and check hoses for leaks with soapy water, never a flame.
**Roasting garri or groundnuts:** use long-handled stirrers and sit or stand so smoke blows away from you. Ventilate well.
**Grinding dry pepper:** wear a face mask, cover your eyes or step back, and wash hands before touching your face. Pepper dust burns eyes and airways.
**Electricity:** keep grinders and sealers away from water and use a proper socket, not joined wires.
Food handler hygiene

Wash hands with soap and clean running water before starting, after the toilet, after touching raw produce or money, and after touching your hair, face or phone. Tie hair back and cover it. Remove rings and bracelets. Cover cuts with a waterproof plaster. Anyone with diarrhoea, vomiting, fever or an infected wound should not handle food until well. NAFDAC asks small food businesses for food handlers' medical fitness certificates when registering, so build this habit now.

Big food companies use formal safety systems. You can use the same thinking at small scale. Two tools help most: the **WHO Five Keys to Safer Food**, a simple hygiene message from the World Health Organization, and **HACCP** (Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points), the internationally recognised method, set out by the Codex Alimentarius Commission, for finding and controlling the dangerous points in a process.

HACCP in plain words

A **hazard** is anything that can make food unsafe. There are three types: **biological** (bacteria, moulds and the toxins they produce), **chemical** (cyanide in cassava, aflatoxin, cleaning chemicals, rancid oil) and **physical** (stones, hair, metal, glass, insect parts). HACCP asks: where in my process could each hazard enter or grow, and where can I control it?
**Conduct a hazard analysis:** list each step and the hazards at that step.
**Determine critical control points (CCPs):** the steps where control is essential to prevent or remove a hazard.
**Establish critical limits:** a measurable line at each CCP, for example oil temperature or a dryness test.
**Establish monitoring:** decide how and how often you check, and who checks.
**Establish corrective actions:** what you do if a limit is missed.
**Establish verification:** regular checks that the plan is working, such as a shelf-life test.
**Establish documentation and record keeping:** write it down every batch.

Check and record
Limit met: continue
Limit missed: correct

Each critical control point runs on a simple loop of checking, recording and correcting.
Worked example: a mini HACCP table for groundnut paste
For example, Halima in Kaduna makes groundnut paste. She lists her steps and hazards.

Sorting raw nuts: hazard is aflatoxin from mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured nuts, plus stones. This is a CCP. Critical limit: no visibly mouldy, damaged or discoloured nuts and no stones after sorting. Monitoring: she checks every tray by eye.
Roasting: hazard is surviving bacteria and moisture. Critical limit: nuts evenly roasted, dry and crunchy throughout when a few are cracked open.
Grinding: hazard is dirt or old residue in the shared mill. Control: she checks the mill is cleaned and runs a small handful through first, which she discards.
Packing: hazard is contamination from hands and jars. Control: washed and dried jars, clean hands, lids closed at once.
Corrective action: any tray with many bad nuts is re-sorted; if mould is widespread the whole lot is rejected.
Halima has one clear CCP (sorting) with a visible limit, plus good hygiene controls at other steps, all on one page she fills in every batch.
Aflatoxin is not removed by roasting

Aflatoxin is a heat-stable poison made by moulds such as Aspergillus flavus. Roasting does not destroy it reliably. Long-term exposure is linked to liver cancer. The control is at sorting and storage: remove bad nuts and keep nuts dry.

Notice that the critical limits in the example are things Halima can actually check with her eyes, hands or a thermometer. A limit you cannot measure is not a limit. For plantain chips a good limit is oil at 160 C to 180 C on the thermometer; for garri, granules that are dry, crisp and free-flowing after cooling; for dried pepper, pieces that snap and pass the jar test.

You do not need to call your plan HACCP or hire a consultant for a home batch. But when you apply to NAFDAC or supply a supermarket, being able to show your steps, hazards, limits and records will make you look prepared and professional, because that is the language regulators and buyers use.

Keep your plan short enough to use. One sheet with your steps down the side, the hazard at each step, whether it is a CCP, the limit, how you check it and what you do if it fails is enough. Stick it on the wall where you work and attach a blank record sheet for each batch. If a step is not a CCP, it still needs good hygiene; HACCP sits on top of basic cleanliness, it does not replace it.

Plantain chips (kpekere in Yoruba) are a popular snack in Nigerian markets, buses, schools and offices. They are a good first fried product because the method is simple and the equipment is common, but quality varies a lot. The difference between soggy, oily chips and crisp, golden ones comes from four things: the right plantain, even slicing, controlled oil temperature and fast, airtight packing.
A bunch of bananas, a close relative of plantain
Firm, unripe plantain gives the crispest chips; ripe plantain gives sweet, softer ones.
Choosing the plantain

Use firm, fully green unripe plantain for classic crisp chips. Slightly ripe (yellow with green) plantain gives a sweeter chip that browns faster and softens sooner. Reject fingers with soft spots, cracks or mould at the stalk. Buy only what you can fry the same day or the next; plantain ripens quickly once cut from the bunch.
The process
Plantain chips workflow
Wash and peel
Slice evenly
Fry at about 170 C
Drain and cool fully
Season lightly
Seal and label
Even slicing, controlled oil heat and full cooling decide whether chips stay crisp.

**Wash** the fingers before peeling so dirt on the skin does not reach the flesh. Cut off both ends, score the skin lengthwise and peel. Unripe plantain sap stains hands, so oil your hands or wear gloves.

**Slice** to an even thickness of about 1 to 2 mm, round or lengthwise. A hand slicer (mandoline) gives far more even slices than a knife. Uneven slices cook unevenly: thin ones burn while thick ones stay soft.
**Heat the oil** in a deep pot to about 160 C to 180 C, checked with a thermometer. Too cool and chips soak up oil; too hot and they burn outside and stay soft inside.
**Fry in small batches**, stirring to separate slices, for a few minutes until the bubbling slows and the chips are crisp and lightly golden. Overloading the pot drops the oil temperature.
**Drain** on a clean wire rack or sieve. Rack draining lets air flow under the chips.
**Cool completely** on clean trays, covered with a clean cloth or net against flies. Warm chips sealed in a pouch release steam and go soft.
**Season** lightly with fine salt (or a small amount of pepper or sugar for variants) while just warm so it sticks, then let cool fully.
**Seal** in clean pouches with an impulse sealer, label with date and batch number, and store in a cool, dry place.
Managing frying oil

Change oil when it turns dark, smells sharp, smokes at normal frying temperature or foams. Old oil breaks down, gives chips a rancid taste and is unhealthy. Strain oil through a fine sieve after each session and store it covered. Keep water away from the pot: even a few drops from wet slices make hot oil spit.

Drying is the oldest and cheapest way to preserve food in Nigeria. Pepper, tomato, okra, ugu, crayfish, fish, maize and groundnuts are all dried. But drying on bare ground or roadsides lets in dust, stones, animal droppings, insects and vehicle fumes, and slow drying in humid weather invites mould. The goal is food that dries **fast, clean and completely**.
A red hot pepper
Well-dried pepper is bright and brittle; mouldy or dusty pepper cannot be fixed by grinding.
Drying methods compared
Open ground drying vs raised rack or solar dryer
Open ground drying
Raised rack or solar dryer
Dust, stones and droppings

Slow in humid weather

Off the ground, cleaner
Covered against rain and insects

Lifting food off the ground and covering it does more for quality than any other change.

A simple **raised rack** is a wooden frame with food-grade mesh or a clean tarpaulin, at least knee height, covered with fine net against flies. A **solar dryer** adds a clear plastic or glass cover over a dark surface so air heats up and carries moisture away through vents. Both can be built locally. Whatever you use, spread food in a thin single layer, turn it at least once a day and bring it in or cover it at night and before rain, because night dew re-wets food.
Preparing food for drying
**Pepper:** wash, remove stalks and any soft or mouldy fruit. Large peppers dry faster if slit or halved.
**Tomato:** wash, slice evenly about 5 mm thick; thicker slices take much longer and may mould.
**Okra:** wash, top and tail, slice into thin rounds.
**Groundnuts and maize:** dry promptly after harvest, sort out damaged, shrivelled and discoloured kernels.
Is it dry enough?

Use the snap test: pepper, okra and tomato slices should be brittle and snap cleanly. Fruit pieces may stay leathery but should show no moisture when torn and squeezed. Then do the **jar test**: put a handful of cooled product in a clean, dry, sealed glass jar for a day. If you see droplets inside or the pieces stick together, it needs more drying. Always cool before testing, because warm food feels drier than it is.
Worked example: drying pepper for a spice blend
For example, Grace in Jos dries 5 kg of fresh red pepper (tatashe and rodo mix) on a raised, net-covered rack.
Day 1: washes, removes stalks, slits large tatashe and spreads in one layer. Weight 5.0 kg.
Days 2 to 4: turns daily, covers at night. Some rodo dry faster; she removes them as they become brittle.
Day 5: all pieces snap. Jar test overnight shows no droplets.
Final dry weight about 0.6 kg, because fresh pepper is mostly water.
She grinds with a face mask on, sieves, and packs in sealed pouches the same day.
Grace learns that 5 kg fresh gives about 0.6 kg dry, which tells her how much fresh pepper to buy for each order and why dry pepper costs much more per kilogram.
Storing dry products
Cool fully, then pack immediately in airtight containers or sealed pouches, before the food absorbs moisture from the air.
Store off the floor on pallets or shelves and away from walls, in a cool, dry, dark place.
Label each container with product, date and batch number, and use oldest stock first (first in, first out).
Check stock weekly for clumping, musty smell, insects, webs or rodent droppings. Remove any affected pack at once.
Never store food next to fuel, chemicals, fertiliser or insecticides.
Do not mix chemicals with stored food

Never add insecticides or other chemicals not approved for food to stored grains, beans or dried food. Some traders do this; it is dangerous and illegal. Use clean, airtight storage instead, such as hermetic storage bags designed for grain.

Good drying and storage protect against aflatoxin too. Moulds that make aflatoxin grow on groundnuts and maize that stay damp or get re-wetted. Fast drying, sorting out damaged kernels and dry, airtight storage are the controls that work.
Buying dried raw materials

If you buy dried pepper, crayfish or groundnuts instead of drying them yourself, you take on the supplier's drying quality. Inspect before you pay. Smell the bag: a musty or damp smell means mould. Look for dust, sand, stones, insects, webs and holes in kernels. Break a few pieces to check they are dry inside. Tip a handful onto a white plate to see dirt clearly. Groundnuts should be plump with clean skins; reject lots with many shrivelled, broken or discoloured kernels. A cheaper bag that needs heavy sorting, or that you must throw away, is not cheaper.

Weather matters too. In the rainy season, drying takes longer and humidity is high, so plan smaller batches, use covered racks or a solar dryer, and pack the same day the food passes the jar test. In the harmattan, food dries quickly but dust is heavy, so keep nets over racks and sieve before packing.

Quality and Evidence: Packaging, Labelling, Records and Costing

A safe product still fails if the pack lets in air and moisture, the label is wrong, or the price does not cover costs. This module covers packaging and shelf-life testing, labelling and NAFDAC registration basics, and the batch records and costing sheet that prove your quality and protect your profit.
Packaging that protects and an honest shelf-life test

Packaging has three jobs: keep the food safe from dirt, insects and handling; keep out the **moisture** and **oxygen** that make dry food soft, mouldy or rancid; and tell the customer what they are buying. The right pack depends on what your product fears most.
What each product fears
Main enemy
Good packaging choices
Garri, dried okra, dried pepper
Moisture from humid air; insects
Thick food-grade polythene or polypropylene bags, double-bagged and heat sealed; airtight tubs
Moisture (loss of crunch) and oxygen (rancid oil)
Laminated or metallised foil pouches heat sealed; thick plastic pouches for short shelf life
Groundnut paste
Oxygen, light and heat (rancidity); contamination
Clean glass or food-grade PET jars with tight lids, stored away from sun
Spice blends
Moisture (caking) and loss of aroma
Sealed foil-lined or zip pouches, small packs so they are used quickly

Thin, cheap nylon is fine for selling garri the same day in the market, but it slowly lets moisture and air through, so it is a poor choice for chips or anything meant to sit on a shop shelf for weeks. Laminated pouches cost more but often pay for themselves in fewer returns. Only use containers sold as food-grade, and never reuse bottles or tubs that held chemicals, oil for engines, or cosmetics.
A closed glass jar
Clean, tightly closed jars protect oily products like groundnut paste from air and dirt.
Sealing well
Wipe the inside top of each pouch so no powder, oil or crumbs sit where the seal will be. Food in the seal line causes leaks.
Set the impulse sealer for your pouch thickness; test on an empty pouch first. Too low gives a weak seal, too high melts holes.
Press out extra air gently before sealing (do not crush chips).
Check each seal: squeeze the pouch, look for gaps, wrinkles or a cloudy, weak line. Reseal or repack failures.
For jars, wash and dry jars and lids fully before filling, wipe the rim, and close the lid at once.
Best before, use by and shelf life

A **best before** date is about quality: after it, the food may be less crisp or fresh but is not necessarily unsafe. A **use by** or **expiry** date is about safety and is used for foods that can become dangerous. Most dry products in this course carry a best before date. Your **shelf life** is the time your product stays safe and of good quality under the storage conditions you state on the label. It must come from evidence, not from copying another brand.
A simple real-time shelf-life test

Week 1 check
Week 2 and 4 checks
Monthly checks

Store sealed samples like a customer would, check on a fixed schedule and set your date before quality drops.

For a **real-time shelf-life test**, keep several sealed packs from the same batch, labelled "Retained sample" with batch number and date, stored in the same conditions a customer or shop would use (not in your fridge). Open one pack at each check. Record smell, taste, texture, colour and any mould, insects or clumping. The day you first notice clear quality loss is your end point. Set your best before date well before it. Laboratories can also run tests, including microbial counts, and NAFDAC's registration includes laboratory analysis of your product.
Worked example: setting a best before date for chips
For example, Kemi in Ibadan seals 8 retained packs of plantain chips from batch PC-05, half in thick plastic and half in laminated foil pouches.
Week 1: all packs crisp and fresh.
Week 3: plastic packs slightly less crisp; foil packs unchanged.
Week 6: plastic packs soft and smell slightly stale; foil packs still crisp.
Week 10: foil packs begin to taste a little stale.
She sets best before at 3 weeks for plastic and 6 weeks for foil, both well inside the point where quality dropped.
Kemi has real evidence for two shelf lives and can decide whether the foil pouch's higher cost is worth it for supermarket orders.
Retain samples from every batch

Keep at least two sealed packs from every batch until after the best before date. If a customer complains, you can open your retained sample and see whether the problem was in the batch or in how the pack was stored after sale.

Packaging also sells. A clean, well-sealed pack with a clear label tells a buyer you take hygiene seriously before they taste anything. A clear window in a pouch lets customers see the colour and crispness of chips or the texture of garri. Keep the design simple and readable on a phone photo, because many of your buyers will first see your product on WhatsApp or Instagram, not on a shelf.

Storage advice on the label matters too: "Store in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Reseal after opening." Shop shelves near a window or a hot zinc roof shorten shelf life, so tell your retailers where to keep your product.

A label is a promise to your customer and a legal document. It tells buyers what is inside, who made it, when, and how to store it. It also lets you trace a problem back to a single batch. In Nigeria, the **National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)** regulates packaged food, and supermarkets, pharmacies and many distributors will ask for a NAFDAC registration number before they stock your product.
A product label tag
A clear, honest label protects your customer and lets you trace every batch.
What goes on the label
**Name of the food**, describing what it really is (for example "Plantain Chips, Lightly Salted").
**Ingredients** in order of weight, largest first (for example "Unripe plantain, vegetable oil, salt").
**Allergens** clearly shown, for example groundnuts (peanuts), wheat, milk, soy, fish and crustaceans such as crayfish.
**Net weight** in grams or kilograms (the food only, not the pack).
**Name and full address** of the producer.
**Date of manufacture** and **best before** or expiry date.
**Batch or lot number** so you can trace problems.
**Storage instructions** such as "Store in a cool, dry place".
**NAFDAC registration number** once you have it.
**Country of origin**: Made in Nigeria.
Never claim what you cannot prove

Do not print health claims ("cures ulcer", "boosts immunity"), "NAFDAC approved" or a registration number you do not have, or a shelf life you have not tested. False labels can lead to seizure of goods, sanctions and loss of customer trust.
Registering your business and product

First, register your business with the **Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC)**, either as a business name or a company. NAFDAC asks for this evidence. NAFDAC has a Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) desk and published guidelines for cottage and kitchen-scale food businesses, so small producers are expected and catered for.
NAFDAC small-scale registration steps
Submit form and documents
Book premises inspection
Samples taken for lab
Approval after GMP and lab
Collect certificate
These are the stages NAFDAC's MSME guidance describes for small-scale food producers.

NAFDAC's MSME "Getting started" page lists documents such as: evidence of CAC registration, a site use agreement for your premises, evidence of trademark approval, three copies of your product label, a fumigation certificate for the premises, payment receipts for inspection, laboratory analysis and registration, and food handlers' or medical fitness certificates for production staff. Payment is made through Remita after you receive a payment advice. The page gives a target of 90 working days for the process. When this course was written, the page listed small-scale food fees totalling about N66,775 (approximate); always confirm current fees and requirements with NAFDAC or your state office before paying, and pay only through official channels.
Beware of 'agents' and fake numbers
Some people offer to 'get' a NAFDAC number fast for cash. Pay only through official NAFDAC payment channels and get official receipts. A fake number puts your goods and your name at risk.

Name: Pure Groundnut Paste (Unsweetened).
Ingredients: Roasted groundnuts (98%), salt. She weighs her recipe to get the percentage right.

Weigh before you print. The net weight must be true for every pack, so weigh a sample from every batch. If your product varies, set the declared weight slightly below your average fill so no customer gets less than the label says. Print the batch number and dates with a stamp or sticker you change for each batch, so you can order a large print run of the main label without wasting labels.

Keep labels readable. Use a font large enough to read without squinting, dark text on a light background, and print that does not smudge when the pack gets oily or damp. If you use stickers on pouches, test that they stay on after a few days in a warm shop. A label that peels off loses your batch number and contact details.

You can start learning and testing before registration, selling to people who know you. But to grow into supermarkets, schools, offices and other states, plan for CAC and NAFDAC from the start. Keep your batch records and shelf-life tests from day one: they make the inspection and application much easier.

Two records turn a hobby into a business: the **batch record**, which proves what you made and how, and the **costing sheet**, which proves you are making money. Both can live in a notebook, a phone note or a free spreadsheet app such as Google Sheets.
The batch record
Batch number and date (for example GP-012, 5 Oct).
Raw materials: supplier, quantity, cost and condition on arrival.
Process checks: CCP readings such as oil temperature, roasting checks, dryness and jar test results.
Output: finished weight, number of packs, rejected or broken quantity.
Problems and corrective actions taken.
Retained samples kept and where they are stored.
A person using a large calculator
Costing every batch shows whether your product truly makes money.
Full cost per pack

Many small producers count only the raw food and think they are profitable. Full costing adds everything a batch uses: raw materials, oil or other ingredients, **packaging and labels**, **energy** (gas, charcoal, electricity or fuel for a generator), **milling or grating fees**, **transport**, a fair amount for **your labour**, a share of **overheads** such as equipment wear and NAFDAC costs, and a **waste allowance** for broken or rejected product.
Building a price from the ground up
Profit margin
Labour and overheads
Packaging and energy
Raw materials
Price stands on every cost layer; skip one and your profit quietly disappears.
Worked example: costing a garri batch
For example, Uche in Imo processes cassava into garri and packs 1 kg bags. All prices are approximate and for illustration only.
Cassava roots for the batch: about N20,000. Yield after processing: about 40 kg of garri.
Grating and pressing service: about N3,000. Firewood or gas for roasting: about N4,000.
Palm oil for yellow garri: about N2,500. 40 thick 1 kg bags and labels: about N4,000.
Transport: about N2,000. Her labour, 2 days valued at about N5,000 per day: N10,000.
Overheads and waste allowance (about 10% of the above): about N4,550.
Total cost: about N50,050. Cost per 1 kg bag: N50,050 divided by 40 = about N1,251.
If similar branded 1 kg bags sell locally for about N1,600 (approximate), a retail price of N1,600 gives Uche about N349 profit per bag on top of paying herself, or about N13,960 per batch.
Retail and wholesale prices

Shops need their own margin. If you sell to a retailer who will sell at N1,600, they may want to buy at about N1,350 to N1,400. Check that your wholesale price is still above your full cost. **Margin** is profit as a share of selling price: (price minus cost) divided by price. At N1,400 wholesale, Uche's margin is (1,400 minus 1,251) divided by 1,400, about 11%. That is thin, so she must watch waste and costs, or aim for bigger orders that bring raw material prices down.

Pack size is also a pricing tool. Many buyers in Nigeria buy small amounts often, so a small pack at a price people can easily pay may sell faster than a large one, even though packaging cost per gram is higher. Cost each pack size separately, because a 40 g pouch and a 1 kg bag carry very different packaging costs.
Re-cost when prices move

Raw food, gas, oil and packaging prices change often in Nigeria. Update your costing sheet whenever a main input price changes and adjust your price or pack size openly, rather than quietly reducing quality.

Look at these numbers every few batches, not just once. A falling yield or rising reject rate is an early warning that something in your process, supplier or storage has changed. Rising repeat orders tell you the quality and price are right.

Keep money records alongside batch records. Use a separate account or wallet for the business, for example a business account with your bank or a mobile money account with OPay or Moniepoint, so that sales and costs are not mixed with household money. Write every sale with date, buyer, quantity and price, and every expense with a receipt where possible. At the end of each month, total sales minus total costs gives your real profit, which is the number that tells you whether to grow, change price or try another product.

The batch does not need to be big. A batch of 2 to 5 kg of finished product is enough to show skill and produce real data.

Take a photo at each major stage: raw material on arrival, after sorting or washing, during processing, cooling, packing and the final labelled packs. Photos are strong evidence and also useful for marketing later. Write CCP readings on the sheet the moment you take them. If something goes wrong, write what happened and what you did. After the batch: test and reflect

Do a quality check on day one: open one pack and record appearance, smell, taste and texture. Ask three to five people outside your family to taste and give honest scores out of five for taste, texture and appearance, plus one comment. Start your retained-sample shelf-life log. Specific is the key word: "roast in smaller batches to stop uneven colour" is useful; "do better" is not.

If you see mould, smell anything musty or rancid, find foreign objects, or a CCP failed and could not be corrected, do not sell or give away the product. Record it as a failed batch, note the cause and dispose of it. A failed batch with a clear lesson is still good capstone evidence.

Keep everything in one place: a folder on your phone with photos named by stage, plus clear photos of your paper sheets. This is your portfolio, and it is exactly the kind of record NAFDAC inspectors and serious buyers like to see.

If you are working with a partner or helper, agree who records which check before you start, and make sure everyone handling food has washed hands, covered hair and is well. Brief them on the CCPs in one or two sentences each, so they know what to watch and when to stop and call you.

**WhatsApp Business:** set up a catalogue with clear photos, pack size, price and a short description. Post to your Status regularly and reply quickly. Accept payment by bank transfer or POS and confirm payment in your banking app before delivery, because fake transfer alerts are a common scam.
**Neighbourhood shops and kiosks:** bring a sample, your price list and your label. Offer a small first supply, sometimes on sale-or-return, and visit on a fixed day to restock and collect payment.
**Offices, schools, salons and hostels:** regular orders of small packs.
**Supermarkets and distributors:** usually need NAFDAC registration, a barcode, consistent supply and invoices. Prepare for these as you grow.

Worked example: handling a complaint
For example, a customer messages Ada in Port Harcourt saying her plantain chips were soft.
Ada thanks her, apologises and asks for a photo of the pack showing the batch number and dates.
The batch number is PC-09. Ada opens a retained sample from PC-09: it is still crisp.
She asks where the pack was bought; it came from a kiosk that keeps stock on a sunny shelf by the window, and the pouch seal looks wrinkled in the photo.
She replaces the pack free, moves the kiosk stock to a shaded shelf, and adds a second seal check to her packing routine.
The complaint is resolved, the customer feels respected, and Ada improves both her sealing and her retailer's storage. Without a batch number and retained sample she would only have guessed.
When to withdraw a product

If you discover a safety problem, such as mould in a batch, a foreign object, an undeclared allergen or a CCP failure that slipped through, stop selling that batch at once. Contact the shops and customers you supplied, ask them to remove it, and replace or refund. Record what happened and why. This is called a **recall** or withdrawal. It feels painful, but it protects people and your long-term name. If the product is registered with NAFDAC, contact the agency for guidance on reporting.

Agree terms with shops in writing, even a simple WhatsApp message: price per pack, quantity supplied, whether unsold stock comes back, when you will collect payment, and where the shop will display your product. Ask them to keep it out of direct sun and to sell older stock first. Check the best before dates on your stock in each shop when you visit, and take back anything close to its date so customers never find expired packs with your name on them.
Collect reviews the right way
Ask happy customers if you may share their message or photo. Never write fake reviews or post others' words without permission. Real, specific feedback is more convincing anyway.

Finally, price clearly and consistently. Use the costing sheet from Module 3, show the same price to everyone for the same quantity, and explain changes honestly when input prices rise. Customers forgive a price increase they understand far more easily than a pack that quietly gets smaller.

Delivery is part of the product. Pack orders in a clean carton or bag that protects pouches from crushing and rain, and keep food away from fuel, chemicals and sharp objects in transport. If you use a dispatch rider, agree who pays for damage before the first trip. Note every order and delivery in your sales record so you know your best customers and areas.

Know your answers before buyers ask. Have a short message ready that says what the product is, its pack sizes and prices, how long it keeps once opened, how to store it, how to order and how to pay. Paste the same accurate message every time so nothing important is forgotten or exaggerated.

Is it ready to sell?

Be honest. A 90-day plan
Days 1-30: repeat and refine
Days 31-60: test and sell
Days 61-90: decide and formalise

**Days 31 to 60:** sell to a small, steady group (neighbours, colleagues, one or two shops). Track repeat buyers, complaints and yield. Continue shelf-life checks.

Ways to keep growing
Join or form a cooperative to share equipment such as a grater, press, solar dryer or sealer and to buy packaging in bulk.

Learn bookkeeping basics so you know your real monthly profit.

Growth brings new tasks. More volume means buying raw materials in bulk and storing them safely, possibly hiring a helper who must be trained in hygiene and your CCPs, and keeping stricter stock records. Grow in steps you can control, and re-check your costing at each new volume, because bulk buying lowers some costs while extra labour and storage raise others.
Safety does not scale down
Whether you make 2 kg or 200 kg, the same hygiene rules, CCPs and honesty apply. As you grow, the stakes grow too, because more people eat your food.

You started this course with cheap, perishable harvests. You now have a method to turn them into safe, labelled, costed products with evidence to back every claim. That combination of skill, records and honesty is what makes a small food business last.

Why food spoils
Three reasons food goes bad
Bacteria, moulds and yeasts feed on the moisture and nutrients in food.
Enzymes inside the food keep working after harvest, softening and browning it.
Insects, rodents and bruising open the door to both.
Fresh food spoils for three main reasons. First, microorganisms: bacteria, moulds and yeasts feed on the moisture and nutrients in food.
They need water, food, warmth and time. Every method you learn takes away at least one of these.
Second, enzymes inside the food keep working after harvest, softening and browning it.
Third, pests and physical damage, like insects, rats and bruising, open the door to both.
The science
How processing stops spoilage
Water: dry it until it snaps or crunches
Heat: kills microbes and stops enzymes
Acid: slows bacteria, like sour garri
Salt and sugar: bind the water
Water is the most important factor. Properly dried foods keep. Dried pepper should snap, not bend. Garri should flow freely. Chips should crunch, not chew.
If a product bends or feels leathery, there is still enough water for mould.
Heat, from roasting or frying, kills most microorganisms. But once food cools and is exposed again, only good packaging protects it.
Acid slows bacteria. Fermented garri becomes slightly sour, which helps it keep.
Salt and sugar both pull water away from microbes.
Step by step
Never rush pressing or roasting: water and cyanide stay behind.
Peel and wash within a day or two
Grate into a fine mash
Bag, ferment and press, 1 to 3 days
Sieve the pressed cake
Roast on steady heat, stirring
Cool fully, sieve and pack
Garri shows the science clearly. Cassava contains natural compounds that can release cyanide, and each step has a job.
Peel and wash within a day or two of harvest, because the roots rot fast.
Grate into a fine mash. This lets the natural enzymes start breaking down the cyanide compounds.
Bag, ferment and press, usually for one to three days. The liquid drains out and takes some cyanide with it.
Sieve the cake to remove fibre and lumps.
Roast in a wide pan on steady heat, stirring constantly until dry and crisp.
Cool fully before packing, because packing warm causes mould.
For example, Bisi pressed for only half a day and roasted on high heat. Her garri went lumpy and stale. Next time she pressed for two full days and roasted on medium heat.

Food safety
The WHO Five Keys to Safer Food
Cook thoroughly
The World Health Organization gives five keys to safer food. First, keep clean. Wash hands and tools, and keep insects, rats and pets out.
Second, separate raw and cooked. Use separate bowls, trays and boards.
Third, cook thoroughly. Roast and fry until fully done inside, not just browned outside.
Fourth, keep food at safe temperatures. Between 5 C and 60 C, bacteria multiply fast. Do not leave moist cooked food out for more than 2 hours.
Fifth, use safe water, and reject mouldy or damaged raw food.
HACCP made simple
Find and control the danger points
A limit you cannot measure is not a limit.
List each step and its hazards
Pick the critical control points
Set a limit you can check
Decide the check and the correction
Record it every batch
HACCP means Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points. A hazard is anything that can make food unsafe: biological, like mould; chemical, like aflatoxin or cyanide; or physical, like stones or hair.
Next, pick the critical control points. These are the steps where control is essential.
At each one, set a critical limit you can check with your eyes, hands or a thermometer. For chips, oil at 160 C to 180 C.
Decide how often you check it, and what you do if the limit is missed.
And write it down every batch, on one page you stick on the wall.
Worked example
Halima's groundnut paste plan
No mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured nuts and no stones. Checks every tray by eye.
Cracks a few nuts open: evenly roasted, dry and crunchy throughout.
Checks the shared mill is clean, runs a small handful through first and discards it.
For example, Halima in Kaduna makes groundnut paste. Her main danger is aflatoxin, a poison made by moulds. Roasting does not destroy it reliably, and long-term exposure is linked to liver cancer.
So her critical control point is sorting. Her limit: no mouldy, shrivelled or discoloured nuts, and no stones. If mould is widespread, the whole lot is rejected.
At roasting, she cracks a few nuts open to check they are dry and crunchy throughout.
At grinding, she checks the shared mill is clean, and runs a small handful through first, then throws it away.

A plantain chips batch
Cool chips completely before sealing, or they go soft.
Firm green plantain, washed and peeled
Slice evenly, 1 to 2 mm
Heat oil to 160 C to 180 C

Now a full chips batch. Use firm, fully green plantain. Wash before peeling, and oil your hands or wear gloves against the sap.
Slice evenly, about 1 to 2 mm. A hand slicer works far better than a knife. Thin slices burn while thick ones stay soft.

Fry in small batches. Overloading the pot drops the oil temperature.

Keep water away from hot oil, and change oil when it turns dark, smells sharp or smokes.

Why this matters

You can make a safe product and still fail. The pack may let in moisture and oxygen, which make dry food soft, mouldy or rancid.
The label may be wrong.
Or the price may not cover your costs.
This module shows you how to protect your product, label it honestly, and keep records that prove your quality and your profit.
Step by step
Food in the seal line causes leaks.
Wipe the inside top of each pouch
Test the sealer on an empty pouch
Press out extra air gently
Squeeze and check every seal
Jars: wash, dry, wipe rim, close at once
Choose packaging for what your product fears most. Chips fear moisture and oxygen, so laminated foil pouches protect them best. Thin nylon is only fine for selling the same day.
Then seal well. First, wipe the inside top of each pouch so no powder, oil or crumbs sit in the seal line.
Test the impulse sealer on an empty pouch. Too low gives a weak seal, too high melts holes.
Press out extra air gently, without crushing chips.
Squeeze every pouch and look for gaps, wrinkles or a cloudy line. Reseal or repack any failure.
For jars, wash and dry jars and lids fully, wipe the rim, and close the lid at once.
Shelf life
Kemi's real shelf-life test
Keep 8 sealed packs as retained samples
Week 3: plastic packs less crisp
Week 6: plastic soft; foil still crisp
Best before: 3 weeks plastic, 6 weeks foil
A best before date is about quality. A use by or expiry date is about safety. Your shelf life must come from evidence, not from copying another brand.
For example, Kemi in Ibadan keeps 8 sealed packs of chips, half in plastic and half in foil, stored the way a shop would.
She opens one at each check. By week 3, the plastic packs are slightly less crisp.
By week 6, the plastic packs are soft and stale, while the foil packs are still crisp.
So she sets best before at 3 weeks for plastic and 6 weeks for foil, well before quality dropped.

Add the true net weight, your name and address, dates, a batch number, storage advice and your NAFDAC number once you have it.
Stay honest

Do

Confirm current fees directly

Print health claims
Print a number you do not have

To grow into supermarkets, register your business with the Corporate Affairs Commission first. NAFDAC has a desk for small producers. Always confirm current fees and steps with NAFDAC directly.
Never print health claims like cures ulcer, never print a NAFDAC number you do not have, and never pay someone to get a number fast for cash. False labels can lead to seizure of goods.

Naira prices are approximate.
Many producers count only the raw food. Full cost adds packaging, energy, milling fees, transport, your labour, and a 10% allowance for overheads and waste.
Uche's cassava costs about 20,000 naira, and her 2 days of labour are valued at 10,000 naira. Her whole batch costs about 50,050 naira for 40 bags.
So each bag costs her about 1,251 naira.
At a retail price of 1,600 naira, she makes about 349 naira profit per bag, on top of paying herself.
A shop wants to buy at about 1,400 naira. That is still above her cost, but her margin is only about 11%. So she must watch waste and costs closely.
Key points
Remember

Full cost includes labour, waste and overheads
To remember. Choose packaging for what your product fears. Check every seal. Set shelf life from your own retained samples. Label truthfully, with allergens clear.
And keep a batch record and a costing sheet, so your wholesale price always stays above full cost.

Your capstone is one real batch, made with everything you have learned. 2 to 5 kg of finished product is enough.

For example, Zainab in Bauchi buys 3.0 kg of groundnuts and sorts out 0.15 kg of shrivelled, broken and discoloured nuts. That is her critical control point against aflatoxin, and she takes a photo.
She roasts on medium heat and cracks several nuts to check they are golden and crunchy throughout.
She watches the mill being cleaned and throws away the first handful.
She fills 10 jars of 250 g, washed and dried beforehand, and labels them with batch GP-001 and an allergen line.
She keeps two jars as retained samples. She also writes what to improve: skinning by hand was slow.
Safety first
Sell it, or throw it away?
Safe to sell
All CCP limits met
Smells and tastes right
Sealed and labelled
Do not sell
Mould, musty or rancid smell
Foreign objects found
CCP failed, not corrected
On day one, open a pack and check appearance, smell, taste and texture. Ask three to five people outside your family to score it out of five.
If you see mould, smell anything musty or rancid, find foreign objects, or a CCP failed and could not be corrected, do not sell it or give it away.
Record it as a failed batch, note the cause, and dispose of it. A failed batch with a clear lesson is still good evidence.
Selling honestly
Specific facts build trust
Not "best quality chips"
Say: fried at a checked temperature
Say: cooled fully, sealed in foil
Confirm payment in your bank app
Vague words like quality and best mean little, because everyone uses them.
Use specific, truthful facts from your own process. Fried in fresh oil at a checked temperature, cooled fully and sealed in foil pouches to stay crunchy.
On WhatsApp, show clear photos, pack size and price. And always confirm payment in your banking app before delivery, because fake transfer alerts are a common scam.
Complaints
Ada traces a complaint
Thank her, apologise, and ask for a photo showing the batch number and dates.
Open the retained sample from batch PC-09. It is still crisp.
Replace the pack free, move kiosk stock to a shaded shelf, add a second seal check.
For example, a customer tells Ada in Port Harcourt that her chips were soft. Ada thanks her, apologises, and asks for a photo showing the batch number.
It is batch PC-09. Ada opens her retained sample from that batch. It is still crisp. The pack came from a kiosk with a sunny shelf, and the seal looks wrinkled.
She replaces the pack free, moves the kiosk stock to shade, and adds a second seal check.
If you ever find a real safety problem, stop selling that batch at once, contact everyone you supplied, and replace or refund. That is a recall.
Your next 3 months
Ready to sell: three good batches, tested shelf life, a working price.
Days 1 to 30: repeat and refine
Days 31 to 60: test and sell
Days 61 to 90: decide and formalise
In days 1 to 30, make two or three more small batches, changing one thing at a time. Keep full records.
In days 31 to 60, sell to a small, steady group and track repeat buyers, complaints and yield.
For example, Funmi plans to sell 50 g pouches to 15 regular buyers, with a target of at least 8 repeat buyers.
In days 61 to 90, review your numbers and decide: continue, change, or move to CAC and NAFDAC registration.
Your product is ready for wider sale when three batches in a row meet your limits, your samples keep, and your price covers full cost.
